De Brazza's monkey (Cercopithecus neglectus) is a semi-terrestrial guenon inhabiting dense riverine forests of Central Africa. Under the typical body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] characteristic of active catarrhine primates, gestation in this species lasts approximately 177 days [tg = approximately 177 days], a duration that aligns closely with predictions based on maternal body size among cercopithecines. The single offspring produced per birth event has a neonatal wet weight of roughly 260 grams [Wwb = roughly 260 grams], a value that reflects the considerable degree of precociality observed in this genus. Females typically give birth to one infant per year, yielding a maximum reproductive rate that, under optimal conditions, translates to one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. This low annual fecundity is consistent with an extended period of maternal investment and a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival over high reproductive output, a pattern documented in several other forest-dwelling guenons facing relatively stable but resource-limited environments.

Sexual maturation in De Brazza's monkey occurs relatively late compared to many other guenons of comparable body size. At a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], females typically attain puberty at 1,611 days [tp = 1,611 days] after birth, a developmental landmark that coincides with the completion of skeletal growth and the onset of cyclic ovarian activity. Males exhibit an even more protracted period of maturation, with reproductive maturity considerably later at 2,555 days after birth [tp = 2,555 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This marked sexual dimorphism in the timing of reproductive maturity is uncommon among cercopithecids and is hypothesized to relate to the species' social system, in which males must attain a sufficiently large body size and establish a stable position within a multi-male, multi-female group before they can successfully compete for mating opportunities. The extended juvenile period in males allows for continued somatic growth and social learning within their natal groups.

Weaning in De Brazza's monkey, defined as the cessation of regular milk intake, typically occurs at 395 days after birth [tx = 395 days after birth] under standard physiological conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This extended nursing period, lasting well over a year, is among the longest documented for any guenon and is thought to be facilitated by the relatively nutrient-rich, predictable fruit and foliage resources of their swamp-forest habitat. The prolonged dependency interval allows the infant to acquire complex foraging skills and develop strong social bonds with its mother and other group members before nutritional independence. Following weaning, the juvenile continues to associate closely with its mother for an additional period, often until the birth of the next sibling, with dispersal from the natal group typically occurring around the onset of puberty. This extended period of post-weaning association is a hallmark of the species' conservative reproductive strategy.

Captive records provide valuable data on the asymptotic body masses attainable by Cercopithecus neglectus under conditions of consistent food availability and limited predation. Adult females in captivity reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 4,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,100 grams], whereas adult males, exhibiting pronounced sexual dimorphism, attain a much greater ultimate wet weight of approximately 9,153 grams [Wwi = approximately 9,153 grams]. This more than twofold difference in body mass between the sexes is among the most extreme observed within the genus Cercopithecus and is thought to be driven by intense male-male competition for access to receptive females. The male mass of over nine kilograms positions De Brazza's monkey as one of the largest guenons, comparable in size to some smaller baboon species, and this large body size may also function as a deterrent against terrestrial predators such as leopards and large carnivores.

Longevity records from captive populations indicate that De Brazza's monkey has a maximum lifespan of approximately 30.8 years [am = approximately 30.8 years] when maintained under the sustained, thermoneutral conditions typical of managed care, corresponding to a core body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This impressive lifespan is among the longest reported for any Old World monkey of its body size and underscores the species' position at the slow end of the cercopithecid life-history continuum. The low annual reproductive output, extended gestation period (approximately 177 days) [tg = approximately 177 days], delayed sexual maturation, and long lifespan collectively paint a picture of a species that has evolved a conservative, K-selected life-history strategy at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This strategy is well-suited to the stable but relatively low-productivity swamp and riverine forests it inhabits, where the benefits of investing heavily in each individual offspring likely outweigh the advantages of producing more, but less competitive, young.
